title: Pauri 19, sound: asankh naav

segments.voice: Yesterday, neech, the lowly, and countless fools, with Guru Nanak standing among them. Your line was nanak the lowly. Today, the last countless stanza begins.

Names for God, or for whatever people mean by the deepest thing, pile up fast. A grandmother uses one word, a friend another, an old hymn a third. One city street can hold them in several languages, whispered in kitchens and sung behind closed doors. Then there are the places people call holy: rivers, mountains, rooms, a spot under one particular tree. Pauri 19 starts right there, with names and places, and it says both are beyond counting.
screen: `SO MANY NAMES.` → `SO MANY HOLY PLACES.` → `BEYOND COUNTING, BOTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 19 in the original: asankh naav asankh thaav. Four words, two pairs. Asankh you know: countless. Naav, said NAAV, with a long a: names. It's a form of naam, the Name, a word at the center of Sikh life. Thaav, THAAV: places. Countless names, countless places. Hear the rhyme: naav, thaav, the second word landing right on top of the first. It's the third stanza in a row to lean on asankh. Pauri 17 counted devotions. Pauri 18 counted fools. Pauri 19 counts names and places, and then, in paraphrase, goes further: countless worlds, beyond reach, beyond reach. Then a twist. Even to say countless, it says, is to carry a weight on your head. Even the word asankh is too small. Three stanzas built on countless, and Guru Nanak admits that countless isn't big enough either. The same humility as yesterday, turned on language itself. Tomorrow, where the stanza goes next: to letters and words, and why it doesn't give up on them. Today, the sound. Asankh naav, asankh thaav. Said slowly, it opens like a wide room. Said quickly, it keeps time like a pulse. Anyone who recites Japji each morning meets it every day.
screen: `NAAV — NAMES. THAAV — PLACES.` · `NAAV, THAAV: ONE RHYME.` · `A THIRD STANZA OF COUNTLESS.` · `EVEN COUNTLESS IS TOO SMALL.` · then, large: `ASANKH NAAV.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud, asankh naav, asankh thaav: once slowly, feeling the rhyme land, then softer, then almost a whisper. Let it go silent and sit. If you like, let the words ride quietly on your breath, asankh naav on the in-breath, asankh thaav on the out-breath.
Thaav. Places: countless of them, asankh thaav, alongside asankh naav, countless names, and then even countless is called too small a word.
Your line: asankh naav. Countless names, countless places, and even countless too small a word. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Pauri 19 is recited in Japji Sahib each morning; its opening line, asankh naav asankh thaav, is the last of the stanzas built on asankh, countless.

original.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 19, line 1: countless names, countless places.

trapdoor: what you thought: just a list of big numbers.
what it means: names and places are beyond counting, and even the word countless falls short.
what a scholar hears: naav is a form of naam, thaav of place; the stanza's third line, asankh kahahi sir bhaar hoe, turns the humility of Pauri 18 onto language itself.

notes: Naav glossed as a form of naam (name); some read naav here as 'names' of created things rather than divine names. The hook speaks of names for God; confirm framing.
Asankh kahahi sir bhaar hoe paraphrased as even saying countless is a weight on the head; confirm.
Reviewer fix: the script called Pauri 19 the fourth asankh stanza; the asankh run is Pauris 17, 18 and 19 (Pauri 16 opens panch parvaan), so changed to third/three throughout.
